extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of political philosophy; policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A statement of normative criteria for the proper limits of societal authority over individuals — distinguishing self-regarding from other-regarding actions and when society may legitimately intervene. It outlines principles (the 'harm principle'), duties, permissible social penalties, and the roles of education and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty of the individual over himself
rubrics_metrics.description: Each will receive its proper share: to individuality should belong the part of life in which it is chiefly the individual that is interested; the individual is the final judge of his own conduct in matters that concern only himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The individual should have 'perfect freedom, legal and social' to pursue actions that concern only himself. Interference must be grounded on general presumptions and is likely to misapply to particular cases; the danger of misconceived external control outweighs many individual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's authority begins where conduct affects others
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction over it; the question becomes whether interfering will promote the general welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This marks the boundary for legitimate social or legal intervention: when conduct harms others (either through rights-violation or clear public harm), society may consider regulation or punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-injury and bearing a fair share of social burdens as enforceable duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Society may legitimately enforce conduct consisting, first, in not injuring the interests of one another (certain interests being rights), and secondly, in each person's bearing his share of the labours and sacrifices for defending society or its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These obligations can be enforced 'at all costs' on those who withhold fulfilment; they form the core of actionable social duties distinct from private self-regarding conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding actions (the harm principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no room for interference when a person's conduct affects no persons besides himself (all concerned being adult and competent); in such cases there should be perfect legal and social freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central rule: only conduct that affects others falls under society's jurisdiction. Exceptions (children, incapacity) exist; for purely personal conduct, education and persuasion—not coercion—are the appropriate tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment by opinion for hurtful-but-not-rights-violating acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts which are hurtful to others, or wanting in due consideration for their welfare, without violating any constituted rights, may justly be punished by opinion, though not by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social censure and exclusion are legitimate responses to such conduct; they are distinct from legal penalties and operate through reputation and social consequences rather than coercive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite damage or definite risk justifies legal or moral intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever there is a definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, either to an individual or to the public, the case is taken out of the province of liberty and placed in that of morality or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a soldier or policeman drunk on duty should be punished; causing others to suffer loss (debts unpaid, neglect of family) justifies moral reprobation and possibly legal sanction. Vague or merely speculative harms do not meet this threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to oneself are not socially obligatory unless they become duties to others
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called duties to ourselves—beyond prudence, meaning self-respect or self-development—are not socially obligatory, because it is not for the good of mankind that others be held accountable for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-regarding faults (folly, intemperance, lack of self-respect) may warrant loss of consideration but do not constitute moral wickedness or grounds for legal punishment unless they translate into harms or failures of duty toward others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and persuasion preferred over coercion for self-regarding conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence and education should be used to promote the good of others; education works by conviction and persuasion as well as by compulsion, and coercion is an inferior means for influencing personal conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coercive measures in personal affairs tend to produce rebellion and undermine the formation of vigorous, independent characters; therefore society should rely on non-coercive instruments whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascendancy of public opinion threatens individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The ascendancy of public opinion, by levelling social eminences and making resistance to the public will ineffective, creates a mass of influences hostile to individuality and tends toward making people all alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection of individuality requires the intelligent part of the public to value differences and to assert claims of individuality early, before enforced assimilation becomes complete; historical examples and warnings (e.g., comparison to China, fashions) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural social penalties acceptable; active coercion not
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may suffer severe penalties at the hands of others (avoidance, withholding friendship or favors) for faults that concern only himself, but these penalties are natural, spontaneous consequences of faults, not punishments purposely inflicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such social responses—avoidance, cautioning, giving preference to others—are legitimate exercises of others' liberty; they differ ethically and practically from legal penalties or imposed suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regarding conduct that breaches duties to others becomes punishable
rubrics_metrics.description: When self-regarding behavior leads to violation of definite obligations to others (e.g., failing to pay debts, neglecting family, disabling oneself from public duty), it is rightly subject to moral reprobation and possibly punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The culpability lies in the breach of duty to specific others or the public; examples include a family provider becoming incapable through intemperance, or a public servant drunk on duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad example is not sufficient ground for coercion in purely personal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Although bad example may have pernicious effects (especially when it involves doing wrong to others with impunity), when conduct only harms the agent, the example generally displays the painful consequences and thus is more likely to be salutary than injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoking 'bad example' to justify coercion over purely self-regarding acts is weak; interference on this ground risks being misapplied and unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's duty to train the rising generation rather than coerce adult conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has had absolute power over children and nonage and therefore the opportunity and responsibility to train them into rational agents; if it fails, it cannot later justify coercing adults for deficiencies created by neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective prevention of widespread incapacity for self-government lies in education and early upbringing; blaming and coercing adults for failures society allowed to develop is unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference often wrongly applied and breeds counterproductive resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest argument against public interference in pure personal conduct is that, when it does interfere, it will probably interfere wrongly and in the wrong place, provoking rebellion and perverse imitation of the prohibited conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical patterns show coercion of private conduct can produce backlash and fashioning of opposition; thus practical caution is required before extending coercive power into personal domains.
